Auburn University
White Paper Design Documentation
Promoting Electrical Propulsion 24’-25’
Banks Murdock | Henry Kendall | Jacob Nichols
Joey Nashold | Scott Ismert | Wilson CogerIntroduction & Background

Marine vessels were first introduced to the idea of electric propulsion in 1838 in Russia
when Mortiz von Jacobi made a small passenger boat that would transport passengers an
unimpressive 3 miles per hour on the Neva River in Russia [1]. Due to the rise of the internal
combustion engine, it fell in popularity after a brief “golden era” in the early 1900s, but the need
for advanced marine systems that run on clean energy, the inexpensiveness that comes with electric
boat maintenance, and the opportunity to put out more power with less weight have all led to a
resurgence in the concept of electric propulsion for marine applications [2]. To highlight recent
developments and research in electric propulsion, last year in March of 2024, the eWolf tugboat
launched with a 6.2 megawatt-hour battery to be used for propulsion, and the vessel proved to be
significantly more powerful than the diesel tugboats at the same port [3].
What makes electric propulsion unique from other propulsion systems are two design
criteria: power storage and motor selection. Furthermore, considerations for propulsion design,
hull selection, and steering control are also documented within the literature. Decisions made for
all these items were made based on preliminary industry research and a desire to be on the leading
edge of marine technology.
For power storage, batteries are well known and documented as a source of electric power.
In researching different types of batteries, 4 different types of batteries appeared as the most
practical directions: nickel cadmium, lead acid, lithium ion, and lithium polymer batteries. Over
time, lithium polymer (LiPo) batteries stood out due to their popularity in remote control vehicles
and their high energy density [4] [5]. Using a battery in turn made the option of a DC motor by far
the most sensible, so that a converter was not needed to provide alternating current. To reduce
friction within the motor and thus obtain the most optimal motor efficiency, a brushless DC motor
was chosen as the direction for driving the propulsion system [6].
On top of this, hull design and steering control also present themselves as important design
considerations. In 2024’s PEP competition, stability of the hull and steering were both areas of
concern that let down Auburn University’s team in the competition. That meant a new design must
both fit the propulsion design and improve stability in choppy waters on the day of the race.
Furthermore, it must be able to hold competition required weight and the weight of the energy
storage option. Significant research exists on the various hull design concepts, their drag
coefficients, and their ability to remain stable in choppy waters [7] [8] [9]. As for steering, not
much changes as it pertains to design considerations for electric propulsion, but rudder design does
vary in relation to both the hull design and weight, so it does become an area of focus for a team
with the knowledge of the previous vessel having steering complications. In steering, three options
presented as potential options: unbalanced rudders, balanced rudders, jet drive z-axis steering, and
flapped rudders.
Our objective as a team is to design and build a remote-controlled boat to compete and
succeed in the American Society of Naval Engineers’ Promoting Electric Propulsion Competition.
To achieve this goal, we decided that the designing a contrarotating toroidal propeller mechanism
to propel the boat would set us apart and give us an advantage. Following this, our goals were to
select an optimal motor that fit our propulsion design, choose a hull that fit the conditions of the
competition and carries a 60 pound removable payload, design a rudder that gives our boat an
optimal turn radius to reduce our heat time, design a circuit that runs our motor and other electronic
devices at their optimal performance measures, and lastly cool our electronic drive train
components (esc and motor) effectively to prevent overheating.Hull

The team’s approach to selecting the hull prioritized competition's requirements without
compromising the team’s focus on propulsion. As a result, a commercially available design that
aligned with the team's objectives was deemed the most suitable choice. To begin the selection
process, various hull types commonly used in the marine industry were evaluated for their specific
applications. Given the weight requirements, designs such as the hydrofoil and catamaran were
ruled out, as they did not provide the necessary balance of efficiency and stability required for
weight-bearing vessels. Although a catamaran hull was available at no cost from the previous team,
it was ultimately not selected. After careful consideration, the team narrowed the options to two
final candidates: the deep V hull and the planing V hull.
The deep V hull was determined to be the most suitable choice for carrying the required
load while providing stability, particularly in unpredictable sea conditions. The previous year's
competition team encountered issues with water ingress due to both the natural chop of the river
and the wake generated by the trailing boat. To mitigate this risk, the selected V hull features a
steeper deadrise angle, allowing it to cut through wake more effectively. Additionally, its design
enables it to sit higher in the water, reducing the likelihood of water entering the hull through the
cover seal. A 65-inch V hull from a previous build was subjected to weight testing, revealing that
it sat too low in the water, posing a significant risk of submersion. As a result, a larger vessel was
deemed necessary to ensure adequate buoyancy and stability.
Using the drag force equation
𝐹𝐷 = 𝑐𝐷(𝐴)(
𝜌𝑉

where 𝑐𝐷 the drag coefficient, A is the wetted surface area, 𝜌 is the fluid density, and V is the
velocity of fluid, the team found the drag coefficient of a v-hull to use for propeller and motor
calculations. Recognizing the importance of minimizing drag, the team explored hull designs
incorporating chines and strakes. A sharp chine introduces a distinct separation between the bottom
and sides of the hull, preventing water from running up the sides. This reduces the wetted surface
area, thereby decreasing drag. Additionally, strakes—small protrusions on the hull's underside—
promote the formation of air pockets as the vessel moves through water. These pockets further
reduce the wetted surface area, contributing to overall drag reduction.
After taking these metrics into consideration, the 76” Enforcer Scarab was purchased. The
purchased hull and estimated CAD models are shown below in figures 1 and 2.
Figure 1: 76” Enforcer ScarabFigure 2: Isometric and Rear View of Estimated Hull CAD Model

Electronics and Controls
One of the main components the team wanted to improve from previous competition vessel
was the electronics, including power storage and the ESC. The team decided on a larger single
LiPo battery system for the drive using a 44.4V 12 cell battery. Figure 3 below shows the wiring
diagram for the propulsion system including all the parts and safety features.
With a large power supply there are safety concerns. The safety features of the system include the
battery disconnect switch, a Class-T marine grade fuse, and QS8 anti-spark connectors for safety
during installation and use. A supplemental battery system will be used in parallel with the main
drivetrain system to power auxiliary items such as the controller, pumps, and steering servo. One
11.1V battery and one 7.4V battery will be used for this system and are shown in figure 4 below.
Figure 3: Battery and wiring diagram for propulsion systemThis auxiliary system helps avoid complications with a battery eliminator circuit allowing for a

safer and easier process to install and turn on the boat.
The control system selected for our vessel is based around a Futaba R203GF receiver that
is linked to an ESC and servo motor directly, facilitating simple communication between
subsystems.
This system allows for reliable and fast communication between controls and their
respective subsystems without allowing for many sources of error. The receiver comes equipped
with dedicated control ports for the motor / steering servo, eliminating the need for programming
or extra hardware to split control among systems. As the servo motor requires at least 8V of voltage
to run efficiently, and the receiver cannot be powered with an excess of 6V, two LiPo batteries that
are 11.1V and 7.4V respectively have been dedicated to each system. The chosen ESC, the Seal
G2 Series 300A, sports built-in telemetry features such as motor RPM, temperature, current draw,
and voltage among others, which also eliminates the need of dedicated telemetry sensors and a
microcontroller to collect their data. Instead, data collected from the ESC can be directly
transmitted to the vessel’s controller through use of the S.BUS2 protocol built into it, or through a
dedicated Bluetooth app on a mobile device.
Steering
With a larger wetted area of the v-hull, the rudder area needed a large increase from
previously used. The area of the rudder was computed using the equation
𝐴𝑟 = 0.045 × 𝐿𝑊𝐿 × 𝐷
where Ar is rudder area, LWL is the waterline length, and D is the draft of the boat. Using this
equation, the calculated rudder area is 26.05 in2.
Figure 4: Auxiliary systems wiring diagramThe rudder was tested using SolidWorks Fluid Flow Simulation to test for turning force,

and pressure on the faces of the rudder. This helped us to calculate the turning radius, and structure
of the rudder, to withstand the drag forces determined in the simulation. Figure 5 below shows the
simulation results including pressure on the face of the rudder and velocity of the water around the
rudder.
Propulsion
As brushless DC motors are high-speed, efficient (~90% efficiency), and reliable, one was
chosen to drive the drivetrain. In particular, the TFL SSS 56154 motor was chosen due to its high
power of up to 20000W of burst power and 14000w of continuous power, while maintaining
25,000 rpm at 55.5V. To model its current draw and power curves given a steadily increasing
voltage, MATLAB simulations were created in line with the two below equations.
𝑃 = 𝐼 ∗ 𝑉 and 𝑃 = 𝐼

∗ 𝑅
Allowing the power generated to be related to the motor’s current draw and applied voltage.
The results of the simulations can be found below in figures 6 and 7.
Figure 5: Flow Simulation of Rudder DesignThis allows for determining the motor’s peak efficiency voltage by comparing the ratio of

the motor’s power output to its current draw at that point, giving a most efficient supply voltage
of ~50V, meaning the motor is running at its most efficient level at maximum throttle.
Due to the selected v-hull design a shaft drive system was decided on, as a jet drive system
requires a flat bottom for the intake to properly function. It was also decided that two propellers
with opposite rotations would be used, as this would allow for higher torque outputs with less
impact on the stability of the vessel. The opposite rotations stop the propeller from creating a
heeling moment about the longitudinal axis of the boat. This shaft drive system can take two forms,
one being a single shaft contrarotating propulsion system or two separate shaft systems. Both
systems can be used with either type of propeller.
The contrarotating assembly was designed and built by our team. The usage of ANSI
standard limits and fits was used to design the shafts and housing below as well as various additive
and subtractive technology, such as 3D printing, milling with indexable rotary heads, and CNC
lathe equipment. Pictured in figure 8 is the first iteration of the gear box assembly, of which 3 more
versions were designed.
The second design was essentially a beefed-up version of the assembly pictured above. The
main issue with the second and first design was the height of the propellers. The flat bottom would
not allow for the propellers to interact with non-turbulent water.
Figure 8: First iteration of gearbox design
Figure 6: Motor Power vs Voltage Applied Figure 7: Motor Current Draw vs Voltage AppliedThe third iteration had an angled housing and longer shafts allowing for the propellers to

reach deeper under the hull. The problems with this design came during manufacturing. Due to the
length of the shafts multiple cutting cycles were required on the mill. This inevitably allowed for
imperfections in surface finish which in turn unbalanced the shafts.
The final assembly was a pod system, shown in figure 9. The pod allowed for the propellers
to be in a constant wet area below the boat while also allowing for shorter shafts. Fluid flow study
showed that the pod could be 3D printed reliably and still have a safety factor of 4 at 60 mph while
propelling the boat. Custom drive dogs were also created and sealed bearings were pressed onto
the shafts.

The design had a single fatal flaw. The gear system was reformatted to fit the housing, but
the gear ratio was still the original ratio purchased at the beginning of the project. The 2:1 gear
ratio prior had no effect, but due to inputting power into the original transfer gear shown in figure
9 on the far right above the system would be outputting close to 40,000 rpm per propeller with our
current motor. Although the system functions fully, the efficiency with our current equipment
would be very poor.
The propellers to go with this contra-rotating design were toroidal propellers, which are a
new design in the world of marine propulsion. The first thing that was seen through research is
that the toroidal propeller is not able to achieve the top speeds that a three-blade propeller is
capable of. Although it is not able to achieve quite the same top speed, it is much faster through
the mid-range RPMs. This is because of its improved planing ability which will allow the vessel
to accelerate quickly out of the corners of the course and reach top speed faster. This also helps
dramatically with efficiency. It allows for much less power usage to achieve cruising speeds. This
will help to maintain the battery charge and complete the entire course.
The propellers were designed to be mirrored copies of each other. To begin the design, an
airfoil had to be selected. This requires finding the Reynolds Number at the hub using the equation
below.

chord length of the airfoil, which is dependent on the hub size, and 𝜇 is the kinematic viscosity of
water. The hub was made to be 2.26 centimeters. This allows for a chord length of 1.524

was selected to be used as a basis for the shape of the propeller. Its shape is plotted below in figure
10.
This airfoil was selected because it is a flat-bottom airfoil which is commonly used for
marine propeller shapes. This propeller has good performance and coefficient of lift between the
Reynolds Numbers of 500,000 and 1,000,000 as seen in figure 11 showing the coefficient of lift
on the vertical axis and the angle of attack on the horizontal axis of the N10 airfoil.
The plot above also allowed us to choose the relative angle of attack of 8º as this allows
for the highest coefficient of lift before stalling the airfoil. The relative angle of attack is added to
the angle created by the total velocity vector or the sum of the velocity vectors of the rotational
velocity of the airfoil and linear velocity of the propeller through the water. This gave the total
angle of attack of 26º at the hub portion of the toroidal loop.

 The team decided on a propeller that was 7.62 centimeters in total diameter. The pitch ratio

(pitch/diameter) for this type of vessel carrying a payload was assumed to be about 0.9. This allows
the vessel to move quickly but output a high enough force to overcome the extra drag that a heavier
boat faces. Using the specifications above, the following propeller was created using SolidWorks
and is pictured in figure 12.
The pitch of this propeller was calculated using the equation below
𝑃𝑃 = 𝐶𝑇 ∗ tan (𝜃)
where 𝑃𝑃 is propeller pitch, 𝐶𝑇 is, the circumference of the toroidal loop (the path the midpoint of
the blade as the propeller makes one rotation), and 𝜃 is the angle of the roots of the blade. This
pitch will give the propellers a pitch ratio of 0.983.
Using SolidWorks Flow Simulation this propeller was tested and improved. However, after
many attempts, the propeller could not be optimized at the high speeds of the selected motor. Lack
of research into this type of propeller made it very difficult to optimize parameters of the design.
In figure 13 below, the flow trajectory of the propeller is shown. The simulation was run at 2100
radians per second, the loaded angular velocity of the motor.
Figure 12: Toroidal propeller model
Figure 13: Flow Simulation Results for Toroidal PropellerAs seen in the figure 13 above, the propeller succeeds at providing suction and an area of

low pressure at the inlet of the propeller, however it is unable to direct the water into a highpressure stream at the outlet at this speed. Although the design worked in theory and a prototype
was built and made to work, it was not compatible with the selected motor, which was selected for
its speed. This design is made obsolete by a simpler design that allows the propeller to spin faster
and for the vessel to have a higher velocity.
Lack of time caused the group to choose a simpler solution. The group decided to use a
common single flex cable common in remote control boats. This system will consist of a single
1/4-inch flex cable through a 5/16-inch stuffing tube. The tube will start at a 30º angle and exit 8
inches from the stern of the vessel. The shaft will bend to a 10º angle and will continue just past
the stern of the boat. A 67mm 3 blade propeller was selected to propel the vessel. This propeller
has a pitch of 4.49 inches.
Cooling System
After reviewing information from previous PEP competitions cooling was identified as a
key constraint early in the design process, as significant heat generation from the motor, ESC, and
gearbox were anticipated to be limiting factors during the race. In order to manage the thermal
load efficiently, water cooling was selected due to water’s substantially greater thermal capacity
compared to air.
Cooling System Testing Data Analysis and Calculations

These equations and calculations demonstrate that the pump testing data yields an average
cooling capacity of approximately 940 BTU/h. This experimentally derived value was
subsequently integrated into the thermal model for the cooling system, ensuring that the design is
robust enough to manage the significant heat generation expected during the race.
Cooling Risk Assessment
This capacity was then integrated into the thermal model to assess the cooling system’s
ability to manage waste heat generated by the motor. At the motor’s maximum continuous output
of 14,000 W with a standard brushless 90% efficiency, the motor generates about 1,556 W of waste
heat (approximately 5,308 BTU/h). After subtracting the cooling system’s capacity, the net heat
accumulation was estimated to be around 4,368 BTU/h. Using research on standards for brushless
DC motors an allowable temperature rise of 40°F was determined; corresponding to an absorption
capacity of roughly 4,000 BTU (assuming an effective thermal capacity of 100 BTU/°F), our
calculations indicated that the system could maintain safe operating temperatures for
approximately 55 minutes under these conditions.This integrated approach, pictured above in figure 15, informed the design of the overall

cooling infrastructure and will ensure safe operation under race conditions. The craft should be
able to maintain maximum performance without thermal issues or throttling.
Testing
In order to make the prototyping phase as easy as possible and ensure a smooth prototyping
process, we decided as a team that each subsystem of the boat would be individually tested before
being integrated with other systems. Depending on what is needed out of the test, a local swimming
pool in Auburn has been used, but nearby Lake Martin is also a viable option for testing, located
just over a half hour outside of Auburn.
For the hull design testing, we used the local swimming pool, sandbags to imitate weight,
and a force gauge to determine our coefficient of drag for the hull shape. On top of this, we ensured
watertight sealing, buoyancy, and stability of the hull to ensure our theory that a deep-v hull was
the correct choice.
Figure 7: Heat management diagramFigure 15: Heat
management diagramTo test our propulsion prototypes, a drill and shaft setup like the one in figure 16 below

was used in a tank of water to justify SolidWorks flow simulation results and test the durability of
the prototypes that were made. By doing this, we affirmed that our propulsion system will push
water as desired to propel our boat forwards, and we mitigate the risk of not being able to qualify
for the competition because we can’t propel the boat.
In terms of other risks we mitigated with testing, we ensured that the cooling system
worked as expected by setting it up outside of the boat, with a tank full of water to pull from and
beakers to discharge water into after it ran through the cooling system. By doing this, we ensured
that our vessel will not fall victim to the same overheating issue that last year’s team ran into during
the race.
Future Directions
The aforementioned simulation results and calculations showed that for the speed of our
motor, our toroidal propellor design did not perform well. Though the outcome of this analysis was
undesirable, empirical testing is required to verify any simulations/calculations. The newest
propellor design requires testing to ensure that adequate force is being. generated to propel the
boat.
The high max RPM of the motor is efficient, but the high angular velocity of the motor
does not work with any propellor design that has been analyzed. To this end, further ESC
programming must be done and tested prior to the competition to optimize the vessel’s
performance. Through live water testing with the full assembly, we will then assure that the motor
will not exceed the capabilities of the ESC or battery.
There also exist a multitude of longer-term improvements that could be undertaken by
future Auburn P.E.P. teams. Given further research, time, and experimentation, the contrarotating
toroidal propellor drivetrain could be attempted and optimized, allowing for a watercraft that is
not only competitive, but also maximizes on the opportunities presented by the newest cutting edge
propellor technology and research. The hull’s design could also be further optimized, especially if
Figure 8: Propeller testing apparatusFigure 16:
Propeller testing apparatusone would be custom-built rather than commercially purchased. Such a hull could allow for more

efficient geometry and easier planing, while also being designed to accommodate any gearboxes
or drivetrain components required for toroidal propellors. If we had to do it again, we would have
finalized a toroidal propellor design earlier, found out what the optimal angular velocity for it was,
and then purchased a motor and gearbox that fit the needs of the contrarotating propellor design.References

White Paper Design Documentation
Promoting Electrical Propulsion 24’-25’
Banks Murdock | Henry Kendall | Jacob Nichols
Joey Nashold | Scott Ismert | Wilson CogerIntroduction & Background
Marine vessels were first introduced to the idea of electric propulsion in 1838 in Russia
when Mortiz von Jacobi made a small passenger boat that would transport passengers an
unimpressive 3 miles per hour on the Neva River in Russia [1]. Due to the rise of the internal
combustion engine, it fell in popularity after a brief “golden era” in the early 1900s, but the need
for advanced marine systems that run on clean energy, the inexpensiveness that comes with electric
boat maintenance, and the opportunity to put out more power with less weight have all led to a
resurgence in the concept of electric propulsion for marine applications [2]. To highlight recent
developments and research in electric propulsion, last year in March of 2024, the eWolf tugboat
launched with a 6.2 megawatt-hour battery to be used for propulsion, and the vessel proved to be
significantly more powerful than the diesel tugboats at the same port [3].
What makes electric propulsion unique from other propulsion systems are two design
criteria: power storage and motor selection. Furthermore, considerations for propulsion design,
hull selection, and steering control are also documented within the literature. Decisions made for
all these items were made based on preliminary industry research and a desire to be on the leading
edge of marine technology.
For power storage, batteries are well known and documented as a source of electric power.
In researching different types of batteries, 4 different types of batteries appeared as the most
practical directions: nickel cadmium, lead acid, lithium ion, and lithium polymer batteries. Over
time, lithium polymer (LiPo) batteries stood out due to their popularity in remote control vehicles
and their high energy density [4] [5]. Using a battery in turn made the option of a DC motor by far
the most sensible, so that a converter was not needed to provide alternating current. To reduce
friction within the motor and thus obtain the most optimal motor efficiency, a brushless DC motor
was chosen as the direction for driving the propulsion system [6].
On top of this, hull design and steering control also present themselves as important design
considerations. In 2024’s PEP competition, stability of the hull and steering were both areas of
concern that let down Auburn University’s team in the competition. That meant a new design must
both fit the propulsion design and improve stability in choppy waters on the day of the race.
Furthermore, it must be able to hold competition required weight and the weight of the energy
storage option. Significant research exists on the various hull design concepts, their drag
coefficients, and their ability to remain stable in choppy waters [7] [8] [9]. As for steering, not
much changes as it pertains to design considerations for electric propulsion, but rudder design does
vary in relation to both the hull design and weight, so it does become an area of focus for a team
with the knowledge of the previous vessel having steering complications. In steering, three options
presented as potential options: unbalanced rudders, balanced rudders, jet drive z-axis steering, and
flapped rudders.
Our objective as a team is to design and build a remote-controlled boat to compete and
succeed in the American Society of Naval Engineers’ Promoting Electric Propulsion Competition.
To achieve this goal, we decided that the designing a contrarotating toroidal propeller mechanism
to propel the boat would set us apart and give us an advantage. Following this, our goals were to
select an optimal motor that fit our propulsion design, choose a hull that fit the conditions of the
competition and carries a 60 pound removable payload, design a rudder that gives our boat an
optimal turn radius to reduce our heat time, design a circuit that runs our motor and other electronic
devices at their optimal performance measures, and lastly cool our electronic drive train
components (esc and motor) effectively to prevent overheating.Hull
The team’s approach to selecting the hull prioritized competition's requirements without
compromising the team’s focus on propulsion. As a result, a commercially available design that
aligned with the team's objectives was deemed the most suitable choice. To begin the selection
process, various hull types commonly used in the marine industry were evaluated for their specific
applications. Given the weight requirements, designs such as the hydrofoil and catamaran were
ruled out, as they did not provide the necessary balance of efficiency and stability required for
weight-bearing vessels. Although a catamaran hull was available at no cost from the previous team,
it was ultimately not selected. After careful consideration, the team narrowed the options to two
final candidates: the deep V hull and the planing V hull.
The deep V hull was determined to be the most suitable choice for carrying the required
load while providing stability, particularly in unpredictable sea conditions. The previous year's
competition team encountered issues with water ingress due to both the natural chop of the river
and the wake generated by the trailing boat. To mitigate this risk, the selected V hull features a
steeper deadrise angle, allowing it to cut through wake more effectively. Additionally, its design
enables it to sit higher in the water, reducing the likelihood of water entering the hull through the
cover seal. A 65-inch V hull from a previous build was subjected to weight testing, revealing that
it sat too low in the water, posing a significant risk of submersion. As a result, a larger vessel was
deemed necessary to ensure adequate buoyancy and stability.

incorporating chines and strakes. A sharp chine introduces a distinct separation between the bottom
and sides of the hull, preventing water from running up the sides. This reduces the wetted surface
area, thereby decreasing drag. Additionally, strakes—small protrusions on the hull's underside—
promote the formation of air pockets as the vessel moves through water. These pockets further
reduce the wetted surface area, contributing to overall drag reduction.

Electronics and Controls
One of the main components the team wanted to improve from previous competition vessel
was the electronics, including power storage and the ESC. The team decided on a larger single
LiPo battery system for the drive using a 44.4V 12 cell battery. Figure 3 below shows the wiring
diagram for the propulsion system including all the parts and safety features.
With a large power supply there are safety concerns. The safety features of the system include the
battery disconnect switch, a Class-T marine grade fuse, and QS8 anti-spark connectors for safety
during installation and use. A supplemental battery system will be used in parallel with the main
drivetrain system to power auxiliary items such as the controller, pumps, and steering servo. One
11.1V battery and one 7.4V battery will be used for this system and are shown in figure 4 below.
Figure 3: Battery and wiring diagram for propulsion systemThis auxiliary system helps avoid complications with a battery eliminator circuit allowing for a
safer and easier process to install and turn on the boat.
The control system selected for our vessel is based around a Futaba R203GF receiver that
is linked to an ESC and servo motor directly, facilitating simple communication between
subsystems.
This system allows for reliable and fast communication between controls and their
respective subsystems without allowing for many sources of error. The receiver comes equipped
with dedicated control ports for the motor / steering servo, eliminating the need for programming
or extra hardware to split control among systems. As the servo motor requires at least 8V of voltage
to run efficiently, and the receiver cannot be powered with an excess of 6V, two LiPo batteries that
are 11.1V and 7.4V respectively have been dedicated to each system. The chosen ESC, the Seal
G2 Series 300A, sports built-in telemetry features such as motor RPM, temperature, current draw,
and voltage among others, which also eliminates the need of dedicated telemetry sensors and a
microcontroller to collect their data. Instead, data collected from the ESC can be directly
transmitted to the vessel’s controller through use of the S.BUS2 protocol built into it, or through a
dedicated Bluetooth app on a mobile device.

power of up to 20000W of burst power and 14000w of continuous power, while maintaining
25,000 rpm at 55.5V. To model its current draw and power curves given a steadily increasing
voltage, MATLAB simulations were created in line with the two below equations.

Due to the selected v-hull design a shaft drive system was decided on, as a jet drive system
requires a flat bottom for the intake to properly function. It was also decided that two propellers
with opposite rotations would be used, as this would allow for higher torque outputs with less
impact on the stability of the vessel. The opposite rotations stop the propeller from creating a
heeling moment about the longitudinal axis of the boat. This shaft drive system can take two forms,
one being a single shaft contrarotating propulsion system or two separate shaft systems. Both
systems can be used with either type of propeller.
The contrarotating assembly was designed and built by our team. The usage of ANSI
standard limits and fits was used to design the shafts and housing below as well as various additive
and subtractive technology, such as 3D printing, milling with indexable rotary heads, and CNC
lathe equipment. Pictured in figure 8 is the first iteration of the gear box assembly, of which 3 more
versions were designed.
The second design was essentially a beefed-up version of the assembly pictured above. The
main issue with the second and first design was the height of the propellers. The flat bottom would
not allow for the propellers to interact with non-turbulent water.

reach deeper under the hull. The problems with this design came during manufacturing. Due to the
length of the shafts multiple cutting cycles were required on the mill. This inevitably allowed for
imperfections in surface finish which in turn unbalanced the shafts.
The final assembly was a pod system, shown in figure 9. The pod allowed for the propellers
to be in a constant wet area below the boat while also allowing for shorter shafts. Fluid flow study
showed that the pod could be 3D printed reliably and still have a safety factor of 4 at 60 mph while
propelling the boat. Custom drive dogs were also created and sealed bearings were pressed onto
the shafts.
The design had a single fatal flaw. The gear system was reformatted to fit the housing, but
the gear ratio was still the original ratio purchased at the beginning of the project. The 2:1 gear
ratio prior had no effect, but due to inputting power into the original transfer gear shown in figure
9 on the far right above the system would be outputting close to 40,000 rpm per propeller with our
current motor. Although the system functions fully, the efficiency with our current equipment
would be very poor.
The propellers to go with this contra-rotating design were toroidal propellers, which are a
new design in the world of marine propulsion. The first thing that was seen through research is
that the toroidal propeller is not able to achieve the top speeds that a three-blade propeller is
capable of. Although it is not able to achieve quite the same top speed, it is much faster through
the mid-range RPMs. This is because of its improved planing ability which will allow the vessel
to accelerate quickly out of the corners of the course and reach top speed faster. This also helps
dramatically with efficiency. It allows for much less power usage to achieve cruising speeds. This
will help to maintain the battery charge and complete the entire course.

Lack of time caused the group to choose a simpler solution. The group decided to use a
common single flex cable common in remote control boats. This system will consist of a single
1/4-inch flex cable through a 5/16-inch stuffing tube. The tube will start at a 30º angle and exit 8
inches from the stern of the vessel. The shaft will bend to a 10º angle and will continue just past
the stern of the boat. A 67mm 3 blade propeller was selected to propel the vessel. This propeller
has a pitch of 4.49 inches.
Cooling System
After reviewing information from previous PEP competitions cooling was identified as a
key constraint early in the design process, as significant heat generation from the motor, ESC, and
gearbox were anticipated to be limiting factors during the race. In order to manage the thermal
load efficiently, water cooling was selected due to water’s substantially greater thermal capacity
compared to air.

These equations and calculations demonstrate that the pump testing data yields an average

Cooling Risk Assessment
This capacity was then integrated into the thermal model to assess the cooling system’s
ability to manage waste heat generated by the motor. At the motor’s maximum continuous output
of 14,000 W with a standard brushless 90% efficiency, the motor generates about 1,556 W of waste
heat (approximately 5,308 BTU/h). After subtracting the cooling system’s capacity, the net heat
accumulation was estimated to be around 4,368 BTU/h. Using research on standards for brushless
DC motors an allowable temperature rise of 40°F was determined; corresponding to an absorption
capacity of roughly 4,000 BTU (assuming an effective thermal capacity of 100 BTU/°F), our
calculations indicated that the system could maintain safe operating temperatures for
approximately 55 minutes under these conditions.This integrated approach, pictured above in figure 15, informed the design of the overall
cooling infrastructure and will ensure safe operation under race conditions. The craft should be
able to maintain maximum performance without thermal issues or throttling.
Testing
In order to make the prototyping phase as easy as possible and ensure a smooth prototyping
process, we decided as a team that each subsystem of the boat would be individually tested before
being integrated with other systems. Depending on what is needed out of the test, a local swimming
pool in Auburn has been used, but nearby Lake Martin is also a viable option for testing, located
just over a half hour outside of Auburn.
For the hull design testing, we used the local swimming pool, sandbags to imitate weight,
and a force gauge to determine our coefficient of drag for the hull shape. On top of this, we ensured
watertight sealing, buoyancy, and stability of the hull to ensure our theory that a deep-v hull was
the correct choice.
Figure 7: Heat management diagramFigure 15: Heat
management diagramTo test our propulsion prototypes, a drill and shaft setup like the one in figure 16 below
was used in a tank of water to justify SolidWorks flow simulation results and test the durability of
the prototypes that were made. By doing this, we affirmed that our propulsion system will push
water as desired to propel our boat forwards, and we mitigate the risk of not being able to qualify
for the competition because we can’t propel the boat.
In terms of other risks we mitigated with testing, we ensured that the cooling system
worked as expected by setting it up outside of the boat, with a tank full of water to pull from and
beakers to discharge water into after it ran through the cooling system. By doing this, we ensured
that our vessel will not fall victim to the same overheating issue that last year’s team ran into during
the race.
Future Directions
The aforementioned simulation results and calculations showed that for the speed of our
motor, our toroidal propellor design did not perform well. Though the outcome of this analysis was
undesirable, empirical testing is required to verify any simulations/calculations. The newest
propellor design requires testing to ensure that adequate force is being. generated to propel the
boat.
The high max RPM of the motor is efficient, but the high angular velocity of the motor
does not work with any propellor design that has been analyzed. To this end, further ESC
programming must be done and tested prior to the competition to optimize the vessel’s
performance. Through live water testing with the full assembly, we will then assure that the motor
will not exceed the capabilities of the ESC or battery.
There also exist a multitude of longer-term improvements that could be undertaken by
future Auburn P.E.P. teams. Given further research, time, and experimentation, the contrarotating
toroidal propellor drivetrain could be attempted and optimized, allowing for a watercraft that is
not only competitive, but also maximizes on the opportunities presented by the newest cutting edge
propellor technology and research. The hull’s design could also be further optimized, especially if
